```{python}
#| label: quasar-functions
#| include: false

# The course constants sheet, used by every figure on this page, plus the
# course value of the Hubble constant (see "How far, and how bright").
C, G = 2.99792458e10, 6.6732e-8
MSUN, LSUN, PC, AU = 1.9891e33, 3.83e33, 3.0856e18, 1.4959789e13
MP, SIGMA_T = 1.6726e-24, 6.6524e-25
KMS, DAY, HOUR, YR = 1e5, 86400.0, 3600.0, 3.156e7
MPC = 1e6 * PC
H0 = 70.0 * KMS / MPC          # 70 km/s/Mpc, in 1/s


def r_s(M_g):
    """Schwarzschild radius in cm of a mass in grams."""
    return 2 * G * M_g / C**2


def m_min_edd(L):
    """The smallest mass (g) that can shine at L (erg/s) below its Eddington limit."""
    return L * SIGMA_T / (4 * np.pi * C * G * MP)
```

In 1963 an object that looked like a faint star turned out to be the brightest
thing anyone had ever seen: a point of light two billion light-years away, far
beyond every galaxy then known, giving off the light of a trillion Suns. Within
a few years it was clear that the light came from a region no bigger than the
Solar System, and that only one kind of object could do that. This lecture is
about **quasars**, how they were discovered, how we know how far away and how
bright they are, and the two simple arguments that say their engines are
supermassive black holes, the very objects whose growth we followed in lecture
9 and whose homes we met in lecture 17.

## How to read this lecture

**These notes are the reading for this lecture.** Kutner's §19.4, *Quasars*,
in the Chapter 19 PDF under *Reading Material* in Canvas Files, tells the
discovery story and is optional. The lecture builds one argument, and it is
worth holding onto from the start:

::: {.callout-important title="The idea at the center of this lecture"}
**A quasar outshines a galaxy from a region smaller than the Solar System, and
only a supermassive black hole fed by gas can do that.**
:::

Every tool it needs is one you already have. *Spectral lines* reviews what an
emission line is. *The discovery of quasars* tells how a pattern of shifted
lines gave 3C 273 its redshift. *How far, and how bright* turns the redshift
into a distance with Hubble's law and the distance into a luminosity with the
inverse-square law of lecture 7. *The engine* uses the speed of light to bound
how big the source can be, and the Eddington limit of lecture 8 to bound how
massive it must be, which together leave only a black hole. *Broad lines*
weighs the black hole with the orbits of the gas around it, by the enclosed-mass
formula of lecture 17. *Quasars then and now* places them among the galaxies.

## Spectral lines: a short detour

The spectrum of a quasar was the clue that gave the whole game away, so it is
worth a minute on what a spectrum can look like. There are three kinds, and
which one you see depends on what the light has been through.

**A continuous spectrum**, a smooth rainbow with no gaps, comes from hot, dense
matter: the surface of a star, the filament of a bulb, the inner disk around a
black hole (lecture 16). Its shape is the blackbody curve of lecture 7, and its
color says how hot the matter is.

**Emission lines** come from a thin, hot gas on its own. The electrons in each
atom can sit only on certain energy levels, and when one drops from a higher
level to a lower one the atom gives off a photon of exactly the energy
difference: one wavelength, and no other. A hydrogen atom whose electron drops
to the second level emits one of the **Balmer lines**, in visible light:
H$\alpha$ at $656.3\ \mathrm{nm}$ (red), H$\beta$ at $486.1\ \mathrm{nm}$
(blue-green), H$\gamma$ at $434.0\ \mathrm{nm}$ and H$\delta$ at
$410.2\ \mathrm{nm}$ (violet), and so on, closer and closer together toward
$364.6\ \mathrm{nm}$. An electron dropping all the way to the lowest level emits
a **Lyman line**, in the ultraviolet, and the Earth's atmosphere blocks every
one of them: Lyman $\alpha$, at $121.6\ \mathrm{nm}$, cannot be seen from the
ground. Every element has its own set of lines, so the lines in a spectrum
say what the gas is made of, and, through the Doppler effect of lecture 3, how
it is moving.

**Absorption lines** are the same wavelengths, missing. Put a cooler, thinner
gas in front of a source of continuous light, and the gas absorbs exactly the
photons its atoms can use, leaving dark gaps in the rainbow at the lines'
wavelengths. The Sun's spectrum is a continuum crossed by thousands of
absorption lines from the gas of its own atmosphere.

Lecture 3 used the H$\alpha$ line to measure a speed, lecture 16 used an iron
line to see the inner disk, and lecture 17 used the $21\ \mathrm{cm}$ line to
trace cold hydrogen. Here the lines are hydrogen's, the gas is hot and thin and
in emission, and the whole point is that they appear **where they should
not be**.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## The discovery of quasars

Radio astronomy in the 1950s found hundreds of sources of radio waves on the
sky, cataloged by position, and one problem with most of them: a radio
telescope of the time could not say where a source was to better than a good
fraction of a degree, so nobody knew which, if any, of the stars and galaxies
in that patch of sky was making the radio waves. The 273rd source in the third
Cambridge catalog, **3C 273**, happened to lie where the Moon passes. In 1962
Cyril Hazard and his colleagues timed its disappearance and reappearance
behind the Moon's edge with the Parkes radio telescope in Australia, which
pinned its position to a few seconds of arc [@hazard1963]. At that spot on
the photographic plates was a thirteenth-magnitude object that looked like a
star, with a faint wisp sticking out of it. No star had ever been a radio
source.

Maarten Schmidt took its spectrum with the 200-inch telescope on Palomar
Mountain in December 1962. It showed broad, bright emission lines, and none of
them was at the wavelength of any known line. The puzzle lasted about six
weeks. Schmidt noticed that four of the lines were spaced like the Balmer
series of hydrogen, but every one of them shifted to the red by the same
factor, about 16%. Read that way, the line at $563\ \mathrm{nm}$ was H$\beta$,
the ones at $503$, $475$ and $460\ \mathrm{nm}$ were H$\gamma$, H$\delta$ and
H$\epsilon$, and a fifth line at $324\ \mathrm{nm}$ was a line of magnesium
whose true wavelength, $279.8\ \mathrm{nm}$, is in the ultraviolet, where no
one had ever seen it from the ground [@schmidt1963]. The object had a
**redshift of $z = 0.158$**, larger than that of almost any galaxy then known.
In the same issue of *Nature*, Bev Oke reported an infrared line at
$760\ \mathrm{nm}$, exactly where H$\alpha$ belongs at that redshift
[@oke1963], and Jesse Greenstein and Thomas Matthews showed that a second
such object, 3C 48, had a redshift of $0.37$ [@greenstein1963].

```{python}
#| label: fig-lines
#| fig-cap: "The lines Schmidt identified in 3C 273. Gray marks are the wavelengths at which hydrogen (the Balmer lines) and singly ionized magnesium emit at rest; orange marks are the same lines as they appear in the spectrum of 3C 273, every one $15.8\\%$ longer. The pale band is the range of wavelengths that reaches the ground and the eye. The magnesium line, invisible from the ground at rest, is shifted into it."
#| fig-alt: "A chart of wavelength from 250 to 800 nanometers. A pale band marks visible light from about 380 to 750 nanometers. Six gray vertical marks on an upper row show the rest wavelengths of the magnesium line at 280 and the hydrogen lines at 397, 410, 434, 486 and 656 nanometers; six orange marks on a lower row show each line shifted to the right by about 16 percent, to 324, 460, 475, 503, 563 and 760 nanometers. Thin arrows join each gray mark to its orange partner. The magnesium line's gray mark is outside the visible band and its orange mark is inside it; the hydrogen alpha line's gray mark is inside and its orange mark just outside."
#| fig-height: 3.4

lines = [("Mg II", 279.8), (r"H$\epsilon$", 397.0), (r"H$\delta$", 410.2),
         (r"H$\gamma$", 434.0), (r"H$\beta$", 486.1), (r"H$\alpha$", 656.3)]
z = 0.158

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.4))
ax.axvspan(380, 750, color="#f3efe2", zorder=0)
ax.text(565, 2.72, "visible from the ground", color=INK2, fontsize=10,
        ha="center")
for name, lam in lines:
    lam_obs = lam * (1 + z)
    ax.plot([lam, lam], [1.55, 2.45], color=MUTED, lw=2.5)
    ax.plot([lam_obs, lam_obs], [0.55, 1.45], color=ORANGE, lw=2.5)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(lam_obs, 1.5), xytext=(lam, 1.5),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK2, lw=0.8,
                                shrinkA=0, shrinkB=0))
    ax.text(lam, 2.5, name, color=INK2, fontsize=9, ha="center", va="bottom")
ax.set_yticks([2.0, 1.0])
ax.set_yticklabels(["at rest", "in 3C 273"])
ax.set_ylim(0.3, 3.0)
ax.set_xlim(250, 800)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("wavelength (nm)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the redshift of 3C 273"}
**The question.** The H$\beta$ line of hydrogen is emitted at
$\lambda_{\mathrm{em}} = 486.1\ \mathrm{nm}$ and appears in the spectrum of
3C 273 at $\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}} = 563.1\ \mathrm{nm}$. What is the redshift
of 3C 273?

Lecture 3 defined the redshift as the fractional change in wavelength,

$$
z = \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}} - \lambda_{\mathrm{em}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{em}}}
  = \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{obs}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{em}}} - 1 .
$$

Both wavelengths are in nanometers, so nanometers cancel and $z$ is a pure
number. *Do the units make sense?* A redshift is a ratio, so yes. Then

$$
z = \frac{563.1\ \mathrm{nm}}{486.1\ \mathrm{nm}} - 1 = 1.158 - 1 = 0.158 .
$$

**Every line in the spectrum gives the same answer**, which is what told
Schmidt he had it right: a shift that multiplies every wavelength by the same
factor $1 + z$ is what a moving source, or an expanding universe, does to light.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .resolution collapse="true" title="Think about why every line must shift by the same factor"}
A Doppler shift multiplies each wavelength by $1 + z$, so a line at twice the
wavelength of another is shifted twice as far in nanometers, and the *ratios*
between the lines' wavelengths are unchanged. That is why a pattern of lines
survives a redshift: the Balmer series in 3C 273 has the same shape as in a
laboratory, only stretched. It is also why one line alone can never give a
redshift. A single bright line at $563\ \mathrm{nm}$ might be H$\beta$ shifted
by 16%, or H$\gamma$ shifted by 30%, or something else altogether; it was the
*spacing* of four lines, and then the magnesium line and Oke's H$\alpha$
landing exactly where the same $z$ put them, that settled it.
:::

The new objects needed a name. On short exposures they looked like stars, and
the first ones were radio sources, so they were called *quasi-stellar radio
sources*, soon shortened to **quasars**. Objects with the same spectra but
no strong radio emission were called *quasi-stellar objects*, or **QSOs**, and
turned out to be far more common; today the two words are used
interchangeably. By the time of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey's sixteenth data
release, more than **750,000** quasars had been cataloged [@lyke2020]. The
most distant are seen as they were when the universe was less than a billion
years old, which is where lecture 9's question about how black holes begin
came from.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

## How far, and how bright

### Hubble's law

A redshift is a distance in disguise. In 1929 Edwin Hubble found that galaxies
are moving away from us, and that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it
recedes [@hubble1929]. The relation is a straight line through the origin,

$$
v = H_0\, D ,
$$ {#eq-hubble}

where $v$ is the recession speed, $D$ the distance and $H_0$ the **Hubble
constant**. This is the expansion of the universe: every distance between
galaxies grows with time, so from any galaxy, ours included, all the others
appear to be moving away, the distant ones fastest. The value of $H_0$ has
been measured in several independent ways, which agree to within a few percent
and disagree by a little more than their stated uncertainties: the light left
over from the Big Bang gives $67.4\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$
[@planck2018] and distances to nearby galaxies give $73.0$ [@riess2022]. In
this course we round to

$$
H_0 = 70\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}} ,
$$

which is not on your constants sheet, so write it on it. A galaxy a megaparsec
away recedes at $70\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, one a hundred megaparsecs away at
$7000\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

The recession shows up as a redshift. For speeds well below that of light, the
Doppler shift of lecture 3 reduces to $z = v/c$, so Hubble's law can be
written in terms of the one thing a spectrum gives directly:

$$
D = \frac{v}{H_0} = \frac{c\, z}{H_0} .
$$ {#eq-distance}

::: {.callout-warning title="A caveat: the redshift of a distant galaxy is not quite a Doppler shift"}
A galaxy's redshift is not really caused by the galaxy moving *through* space;
it is caused by space expanding while the light is on its way, which stretches
the light along with everything else. The two pictures agree when the redshift
is small, and @eq-distance is good to about ten percent at the redshift of
3C 273. For quasars at $z$ of $2$ or $6$ it fails, not because the formula
for the Doppler shift breaks down but because the expansion has not been
constant over the billions of years the light has traveled, and "the
distance" to the object has to be defined more carefully. That is a subject
for a cosmology course. In this course we use @eq-distance only for
$z \lesssim 0.2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how far away is 3C 273?"}
**The question.** With a redshift of $z = 0.158$, how far away is 3C 273, and
how long has its light been traveling?

The recession speed is

$$
\begin{aligned}
v = c\, z &= 2.998 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} \times 0.158 \\[0.8em]
          &= 4.74 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$

a sixth of the speed of light. Then @eq-distance, with the units attached:

$$
\begin{aligned}
D = \frac{v}{H_0}
  &= \frac{4.74 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}}
          {70\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}} \\[0.8em]
  &= 677\ \mathrm{Mpc} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ cancel and the $\mathrm{Mpc^{-1}}$ in the
denominator comes up as $\mathrm{Mpc}$. *Do the units make sense?* A distance,
so yes. In centimeters, each conversion written so the unwanted unit cancels,

$$
\begin{aligned}
D &= 677\ \mathrm{Mpc}
  \times \frac{10^{6}\ \mathrm{pc}}{1\ \mathrm{Mpc}}
  \times \frac{3.0856 \times 10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm}}{1\ \mathrm{pc}} \\[0.8em]
  &= 2.09 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{cm} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The light has been traveling for $D/c = 2.09 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{cm} \,/\,
2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} = 6.97 \times 10^{16}\ \mathrm{s}$,
which is $2.2$ billion years. **We see 3C 273 as it was before the Sun and
the Earth had formed.** (A careful cosmological calculation puts it a little
farther, about $750\ \mathrm{Mpc}$, as the caveat above warns.)
:::

### The luminosity of a quasar

A distance is what turns a brightness into a power. Lecture 7 gave the
inverse-square law: a source of luminosity $L$ at a distance $D$ delivers a
flux $F = L/4\pi D^2$ to every square centimeter facing it. Turned around,

$$
L = 4\pi D^2\, F .
$$ {#eq-luminosity}

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: the luminosity of 3C 273"}
**The question.** In visible light, 3C 273 delivers a flux of about
$7 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$ to the Earth. At a distance
of $677\ \mathrm{Mpc}$, what is its luminosity in visible light, in solar
luminosities?

From @eq-luminosity, with the distance in centimeters from the worked example
above,

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= 4\pi \left(2.09 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{cm}\right)^2 \\[0.8em]
  &\qquad \times 7 \times 10^{-11}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}} .
\end{aligned}
$$

The $\mathrm{cm^{2}}$ from the distance cancels the $\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ of the
flux and leaves $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. *Do the units make sense?* A luminosity
is energy per time, so yes. The numbers: $4\pi D^2 = 5.48 \times 10^{55}\
\mathrm{cm^{2}}$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
L &= 3.8 \times 10^{45}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}
     \times \frac{1\,L_\odot}{3.83 \times 10^{33}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}} \\[0.8em]
  &= 1.0 \times 10^{12}\,L_\odot .
\end{aligned}
$$

**A trillion Suns**, in visible light alone: tens of times the light of the
entire Milky Way, from a point that a 1960s photograph could not tell from a
star. Counting the radio waves, the infrared, the ultraviolet, the X-rays and
the gamma rays it also gives off, the total is larger still.
:::

This was the shock of 1963. Objects at the distances their redshifts implied
had to be the most luminous things in the universe by a wide margin. Some
astronomers tried for years to put the quasars closer, by finding some other
cause for their redshifts, and failed: everything about them, from the
absorption lines of gas in front of them at smaller redshifts to the galaxies
they turned out to live in, puts them where Hubble's law says. Kutner's §19.4.3
tells that story.

### Quasar hosts

With a telescope above the atmosphere, the glare of the quasar can be blocked
out and what is around it photographed. @fig-3c273 shows 3C 273 both ways.
Around the point of light is a galaxy, an elliptical larger than the Milky
Way, which the quasar outshines many times over, and from the point a jet
reaches out more than a hundred thousand light-years. **A quasar is the
brilliant nucleus of a galaxy**: the same kind of object we found at the
center of the Milky Way in lecture 17, four million solar masses of black hole,
but far more massive and, for a while, fed.

   formula is reliable; a cosmological calculation gives a larger distance.)

2. If a quasar exactly like 3C 273 were ten times farther away, what flux
   would reach the Earth from it? What would its redshift be, by @eq-distance?
   Would @eq-distance be reliable there?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   The flux falls as $1/D^2$; the redshift, by @eq-distance, grows in
   proportion to $D$.

   A hundred times fainter, $7 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$,
   and $z = 1.58$ by the simple formula, which is well beyond where the
   formula holds, so the real redshift of such an object would be different.
   The point stands: the flux is small, and the luminosity is not.
   :::

3. Hubble's law says every galaxy a distance $D$ away recedes at $H_0 D$. Run
   the expansion backward: how long ago was every galaxy on top of every other
   one, if the speeds have never changed? Give the answer in years. This is
   the **Hubble time**, a first estimate of the age of the universe.

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   A galaxy at distance $D$ moving at $v = H_0 D$ took a time $D/v$ to get
   there, and $D$ cancels. Convert $H_0$ to $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ by writing the
   megaparsec in kilometers.

   The Hubble time is $1/H_0 = 4.4 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{s} = 1.4 \times
   10^{10}\ \mathrm{yr}$, fourteen billion years, close to the universe's
   measured age of $13.8$ billion years.
   :::

## The engine

::: {.panel-tabset .tracks}

### Physical intuition

Two facts about quasars, put together, leave only one explanation. The first
is the luminosity we just found. The second is that **quasars flicker**. The
brightness of 3C 273 changes noticeably from month to month and year to year,
and the brightest quasars seen in X-rays can change by a large fraction within
days; the nearest active galactic nuclei, within hours. For a single star that
would be unremarkable. For something that outshines a galaxy, it is
astonishing, because of a rule that follows from nothing but the speed of
light.

**Nothing can change as a whole faster than light can cross it.** Suppose a
glowing region of size $R$ brightened everywhere at the same instant. We would
not see it brighten at once: light from its near side reaches us first, and
light from its far side arrives later, by the time it takes light to cross the
region, $R/c$. The brightening we see is smeared out over about that long
(@fig-light-travel). So if a source doubles its brightness in a time
$\Delta t$, the part of it doing the doubling can be no larger than
$c\,\Delta t$, however the brightening is organized inside it. A source that
varies in a day is smaller than a light-day, $173\ \mathrm{AU}$, about six
times the size of Neptune's orbit. A source that varies in an hour is smaller
than a light-hour, $7\ \mathrm{AU}$, inside the orbit of Saturn. **A trillion
Suns' worth of light, from a region the size of the Solar System.**

```{python}
#| label: fig-light-travel
#| fig-cap: "Why a source cannot change faster than light can cross it. Left: a glowing sphere of radius $R$ switches on everywhere at the same instant; the light that reaches the observer first comes from the near side, and light from the far side has $2R$ farther to go. Right: what the observer sees. The source's own brightness (dashed) jumps at once; the observed brightness (solid) climbs over the light-crossing time, $2R/c$, as light from deeper and deeper layers arrives. However fast a source changes inside, what we see is smeared over the time light takes to cross it, so a change seen in a time $\\Delta t$ means a source smaller than about $c\\,\\Delta t$."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. On the left, a large pale orange circle labeled R at its radius, with an observer marked by an eye symbol far to the right. Two horizontal arrows run from the circle toward the observer: one from the near edge, labeled 'first light', and one from the far edge, labeled 'last light, 2R over c later'. On the right, a chart of brightness against time. A dashed line jumps from zero to full brightness at time zero and stays there. A solid line starts rising at time zero and climbs smoothly in an S shape, reaching full brightness at a time marked 2R over c on the axis."
#| fig-height: 3.0

fig, (axl, axr) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(5.8, 3.0),
                               gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.15, 1]))

# Left: the geometry.
axl.set_aspect("equal")
circ = plt.Circle((0, 0), 1.0, facecolor="#f9dcc8", edgecolor=ORANGE, lw=1.5)
axl.add_patch(circ)
axl.plot([0, 0.7071], [0, 0.7071], color=INK2, lw=1)
axl.text(0.22, 0.50, "$R$", color=INK2, fontsize=11)
axl.plot([0], [0], "o", color=INK2, ms=3)
axl.annotate("", xy=(3.1, 0.62), xytext=(0.78, 0.62),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=BLUE, lw=1.2))
axl.annotate("", xy=(3.1, -0.62), xytext=(-0.78, -0.62),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=BLUE, lw=1.2,
                             linestyle="--"))
axl.text(1.95, 0.80, "first light", color=BLUE, fontsize=9.5, ha="center")
axl.text(1.55, -1.02, "last light, $2R/c$ later", color=BLUE, fontsize=9.5,
         ha="center")
axl.text(3.35, 0.0, "observer", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5, ha="center",
         va="center", rotation=90)
axl.set_xlim(-1.3, 3.6)
axl.set_ylim(-1.4, 1.4)
axl.axis("off")

# Right: what is seen. A uniformly glowing sphere that turns on at t = 0; at
# time t the observer sees light from the part of the sphere within a depth
# c t of the near side, i.e. a spherical cap of height h = c t.
t = np.linspace(0, 2.6, 400)              # in units of R/c
h = np.clip(t, 0, 2)
cap = np.pi * h**2 * (3 - h) / 3          # cap volume for R = 1
seen = cap / (4 * np.pi / 3)
axr.plot([-0.5, 0, 0, 2.6], [0, 0, 1, 1], color=MUTED, lw=1.5, ls="--")
axr.plot(t, seen, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2)
axr.text(1.55, 0.3, "what the\nobserver sees", color=ORANGE, fontsize=9.5,
         ha="center")
axr.text(0.1, 1.06, "the source\nitself", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5)
axr.set_xlim(-0.5, 2.6)
axr.set_ylim(-0.05, 1.3)
axr.set_xticks([0, 2])
axr.set_xticklabels(["0", "$2R/c$"])
axr.set_yticks([0, 1])
axr.set_yticklabels(["dark", "bright"])
axr.set_xlabel("time")
axr.set_ylabel("brightness")
plt.show()
```

Now the second argument, which runs the other way. Lecture 8 showed that
anything shining by accretion has a ceiling on its brightness, the Eddington
limit: above it, the pressure of the light pushes the infalling gas away
faster than gravity can pull it in, and the source chokes off its own fuel.
The ceiling is set by the mass, $L_{\mathrm{Edd}} \approx 1.26 \times
10^{38}\,(M/M_\odot)\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, so **a source of luminosity $L$
must have at least the mass whose Eddington limit is $L$.** For a quasar, that
is tens of millions of solar masses, at the least.

Put the two together. Tens of millions of solar masses or more, inside a
region the size of the Solar System. A cluster of that many stars packed into
so small a space would have its stars a few astronomical units apart, closer
than the Earth is to the Sun; they would collide and merge within a human
lifetime, and the whole cluster would fall in on itself. Whatever such an
object began as, gravity turns it into a black hole, and a black hole is the
one object that can hold that much mass in that little space and go on
shining. The Schwarzschild radius of a hundred-million-solar-mass black hole
is $2\ \mathrm{AU}$; that of a billion-solar-mass one, $20\ \mathrm{AU}$, the
size of the orbit of Uranus. Both fit comfortably inside a light-day. And
lecture 7 supplied the last piece: gas spiraling into a black hole releases
up to tens of percent of its rest-mass energy as light, ten or more times what
nuclear fusion can manage, so a black hole does not even need very much gas to
shine as a quasar does. Edwin Salpeter and Yakov Zel'dovich proposed this
in 1964 [@salpeter1964], a year after Schmidt's paper, and Donald Lynden-Bell
worked out in 1969 that the engine had to be a black hole and that burnt-out
quasars should be sitting, dark and massive, in the centers of galaxies today
[@lyndenbell1969].

### Mathematical explanation

**The size.** If the brightness of a source changes by a large fraction in a
time $\Delta t$, the region responsible cannot be bigger than the distance
light travels in that time:

$$
R \lesssim c\, \Delta t .
$$ {#eq-size-limit}

The "$\lesssim$" is honest about a factor of two or so: the exact bound
depends on the shape of the region and on how the change spreads through it,
and relativistic motion inside the source can beat it (lecture 22). As a
bound on the order of magnitude it is secure. Its units are
$\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{s} = \mathrm{cm}$, a length, as a size
must be.

**The mass.** From lecture 8, the Eddington luminosity of a mass $M$ is

$$
L_{\mathrm{Edd}} = \frac{4\pi c\, G M m_p}{\sigma_T} .
$$

A source that shines steadily by accretion must have $L < L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$,
and solving for the mass gives a *lower* limit on it,

$$
M > \frac{L\, \sigma_T}{4\pi c\, G\, m_p} ,
$$ {#eq-min-mass}

or, with the numbers put in once and for all,

$$
M > \frac{L}{1.26 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}\, M_\odot .
$$

The units of @eq-min-mass: $\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^{2}}$ on top,
and $\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times \mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}} \times
\mathrm{g}$ below. With $1\ \mathrm{erg} = \mathrm{g\,cm^{2}\,s^{-2}}$, the top
is $\mathrm{g\,cm^{4}\,s^{-3}}$ and the bottom $\mathrm{cm^{4}\,s^{-3}}$, which
leaves $\mathrm{g}$: a mass.

**Compactness.** The thing to compare the size with is the Schwarzschild
radius of the minimum mass, $r_S = 2GM/c^2$ (lecture 1). The bound on the size
from @eq-size-limit is an upper limit; $r_S$ of the Eddington mass is a lower
limit on how big the black hole is. A quasar is a black hole if the second fits
inside the first, and for every quasar ever measured it does, with room to
spare. The ratio $c\,\Delta t / r_S$, the size of the varying region in
Schwarzschild radii, is at most a few hundred for a day's variation and a
hundred-million-solar-mass hole, and at most a few for the fastest X-ray
flickers, which are therefore coming from the innermost part of the accretion
disk of lecture 16.

### Numerical exploration

@fig-size-limit plots @eq-size-limit: the largest a source can be, against
how fast it varies, with the Schwarzschild radii of black holes of
$10^{7}$, $10^{8}$ and $10^{9}\,M_\odot$ drawn across it for comparison. The
two scales are the whole argument. A source that varies in days is a few
hundred Schwarzschild radii across at most, for the largest black holes we
know of, and a few astronomical units of flicker is a few Schwarzschild radii:
the inner disk itself.

```{python}
#| label: fig-size-limit
#| fig-cap: "The largest a source can be if it varies in a time $\\Delta t$, $R = c\\,\\Delta t$ (@eq-size-limit), from an hour to a year, on logarithmic axes. The right-hand scale is the same size in astronomical units. The dashed lines are the Schwarzschild radii of black holes of $10^{7}$, $10^{8}$ and $10^{9}$ solar masses, and the dotted line is the size of Neptune's orbit. A quasar that varies within a day is smaller than a light-day; the black hole that powers it has a Schwarzschild radius well below that."
#| fig-alt: "A chart with logarithmic axes. The horizontal axis is the variability time, from one hour to one year, with ticks at one hour, one day, one week, one month and one year. The vertical axis is the largest possible size, from about ten to the twelve to ten to the eighteen centimeters, with a matching right-hand axis in astronomical units from about 0.1 to 100,000. A solid blue line rises diagonally from about 10 to the 14 centimeters at one hour to about 10 to the 18 at one year. Three dashed orange horizontal lines mark the Schwarzschild radii of black holes of ten million, a hundred million and a billion solar masses, at about 3 times 10 to the 12, 3 times 10 to the 13 and 3 times 10 to the 14 centimeters, each labeled at the right. A dotted gray horizontal line labeled Neptune's orbit sits at 4.5 times 10 to the 14 centimeters. The blue line is above all three dashed lines everywhere except that it crosses the billion-solar-mass line near three hours."
#| fig-height: 4.2

# The black hole and the timescale to mark on the plot, in solar masses and hours.
M_bh = 1.0e8           # mass of the black hole, in solar masses
dt_hours = 24.0        # how fast the quasar varies, in hours

dt = np.logspace(np.log10(HOUR), np.log10(YR), 300)      # seconds
R_max = C * dt                                            # cm

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.55, 4.2))
ax.plot(dt, R_max, color=BLUE, lw=2.2, zorder=3)
ax.text(2.2 * DAY, 2.0e16, r"largest size, $R = c\,\Delta t$", color=BLUE,
        fontsize=10.5, rotation=36, rotation_mode="anchor")
for M, ytext in ((1e7, 1.35), (1e8, 1.35), (1e9, 1.35)):
    rs = r_s(M * MSUN)
    ax.axhline(rs, color=ORANGE, lw=1.4, ls="--", zorder=2)
    ax.text(0.95 * YR, rs * ytext,
            rf"$r_S$ of $10^{{{int(np.log10(M))}}}\,M_\odot$", color=ORANGE,
            fontsize=9.5, ha="right", va="bottom")
ax.axhline(30 * AU, color=MUTED, lw=1.2, ls=":", zorder=2)
ax.text(1.15 * HOUR, 30 * AU * 1.35, "Neptune's orbit", color=INK2,
        fontsize=9.5, va="bottom")
R_pick, rs_pick = C * dt_hours * HOUR, r_s(M_bh * MSUN)
ax.plot([dt_hours * HOUR], [R_pick], "o", color=AQUA, ms=8, mec=INK,
        mew=0.8, zorder=4)
print(f"varies in {dt_hours:g} h: R < {R_pick:.2e} cm = {R_pick / AU:.0f} AU")
print(f"= {R_pick / rs_pick:.0f} Schwarzschild radii of {M_bh:.0e} Msun")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlim(HOUR, YR)
ax.set_ylim(1e12, 1.5e18)
ax.set_xticks([HOUR, DAY, 7 * DAY, 30 * DAY, YR])
ax.set_xticklabels(["1 hour", "1 day", "1 week", "1 month", "1 year"])
ax.set_xlabel(r"variability time, $\Delta t$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"largest possible size, $R$ (cm)")
ax2 = ax.secondary_yaxis("right", functions=(lambda r: r / AU,
                                             lambda a: a * AU))
ax2.set_ylabel(r"$R$ (AU)")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note .worked-example collapse="true" title="Worked example: how small, and how massive, is the engine of 3C 273?"}
**The question.** The brightness of 3C 273 can change by a noticeable fraction
in about a day. How big can the region making that light be, in astronomical
units? Its luminosity in visible light is $3.8 \times 10^{45}\
\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$; what is the smallest mass that can shine that brightly,
and what is that mass's Schwarzschild radius?

**The size**, from @eq-size-limit with $\Delta t = 1\ \mathrm{d} = 86{,}400\
\mathrm{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R &\lesssim 2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}} \times 8.64 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{s} \\[0.8em]
  &= 2.59 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm} .
\end{aligned}
$$

Centimeters per second times seconds is centimeters. *Do the units make
sense?* A size, so yes. In astronomical units,

$$
R \lesssim 2.59 \times 10^{15}\ \mathrm{cm}
   \times \frac{1\ \mathrm{AU}}{1.496 \times 10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm}}
  = 173\ \mathrm{AU} .
$$

**The mass**, from @eq-min-mass. The quick form is enough here:

$$
\begin{aligned}
M &> \frac{3.8 \times 10^{45}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}
          {1.26 \times 10^{38}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}}\, M_\odot \\[0.8em]
  &= 3.0 \times 10^{7}\,M_\odot .
\end{aligned}
$$

The ergs per second cancel and leave a pure number of solar masses. *Do the
units make sense?* A mass, so yes. (The light we counted is only the visible
part, so the true lower limit is larger.)

**The Schwarzschild radius** of $3.0 \times 10^{7}\,M_\odot = 6.0 \times
10^{40}\ \mathrm{g}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
r_S &= \frac{2 \times 6.6732 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm^{3}\,g^{-1}\,s^{-2}}
            \times 6.0 \times 10^{40}\ \mathrm{g}}
           {\left(2.998 \times 10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\right)^2} \\[0.8em]
    &= 9.0 \times 10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.60\ \mathrm{AU} .
\end{aligned}
$$

**Thirty million Suns at least, inside a region at most 173 AU across**, and
a black hole of that mass, a little over half an astronomical unit in radius,
fits inside it three hundred times over. The engine is a black hole. Its real
mass, weighed by the gas orbiting it in the next section, is tens of times
larger than this minimum, which is why 3C 273 shines at only a few percent of
its Eddington limit.
:::

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-engine}

1. A quasar shines at $10^{46}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ for a hundred million
   years. How much energy is that, in ergs? If the energy came from gas
   spiraling into a black hole with a radiative efficiency of 10% (lecture 7),
   how much gas had to fall in, in solar masses? And if it came from nuclear
   fusion, which releases 0.7% of the rest-mass energy of its fuel, how much
   hydrogen would have had to burn?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   The energy is $L \times t$, with $t$ in seconds. Then $E = \eta\, m c^2$
   gives the mass $m$ for each efficiency $\eta$; convert grams to solar
   masses with a conversion fraction.

   The energy is $3.2 \times 10^{61}\ \mathrm{erg}$. Accretion needs
   $1.8 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$ of gas; fusion would need
   $2.5 \times 10^{9}\,M_\odot$ of hydrogen, the mass of a small galaxy's
   worth of stars, burned to completion inside a region the size of the Solar
   System.
   :::

2. At that luminosity and efficiency, how much gas does the black hole swallow
   each year, in solar masses per year? Compare with lecture 9's Eddington
   accretion rate for a $10^{8}\,M_\odot$ black hole.

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   About $1.8\,M_\odot$ per year.
   :::

3. The X-rays of some active galactic nuclei change by a large fraction within
   an hour. How big can the X-ray source be, in astronomical units? If the
   black hole has $10^{7}\,M_\odot$, how many Schwarzschild radii is that?
   Where in lecture 16's picture of the disk must those X-rays come from?

4. Suppose someone proposed that a quasar is not a black hole but a cluster of
   $10^{8}$ ordinary stars packed into a sphere $100\ \mathrm{AU}$ in radius.
   How far apart would neighboring stars be, on average, in astronomical
   units and in solar radii? What would happen to such a cluster, and how
   fast?

:::

## Broad lines: the gas near the engine

The emission lines that gave quasars away have a second thing to tell us. They
are **broad**: not a sharp line at one wavelength but a hump spread over
several nanometers, which is the Doppler effect at work. The light of each line
comes from many clouds of gas, each moving at its own speed, some toward us
and blueshifted, some away and redshifted, and the sum of all their lines is a
single wide one (@fig-broad-line). The width of the hump measures the spread
of speeds, and in a quasar it is thousands of kilometers per second, one
percent of the speed of light or more. Nothing moves that fast unless
something very massive is holding it in orbit very close by. This is the
same reasoning that weighed the Milky Way in lecture 17: **how fast the gas
orbits tells us how much mass is inside its orbit**, $M = rv^2/G$. The speed
is in the width of the line. The radius is the hard part.

```{python}
#| label: fig-broad-line
#| fig-cap: "How a broad emission line is made. Thousands of clouds of gas orbit the black hole, here at speeds of a few thousand kilometers per second, in every direction. Each cloud emits a sharp H$\\beta$ line at $486.1\\ \\mathrm{nm}$, Doppler shifted by its own motion along our line of sight (a few of them are drawn as thin lines). Their sum, the orange hump, is the broad line that is observed; its width across the middle corresponds here to about $5000\\ \\mathrm{km\\,s^{-1}}$. The narrow blue line is what gas moving at a few hundred kilometers per second would give instead, the width of the lines of a quiet galaxy."
#| fig-alt: "A chart of brightness against wavelength near 486 nanometers, with a matching scale of velocity from minus 8000 to plus 8000 kilometers per second along the top. A broad, smooth orange hump spans from about 480 to 492 nanometers, with a horizontal bar across its middle labeled width. Under the hump, about a dozen faint thin spikes mark the sharp lines of individual clouds at scattered wavelengths. A tall narrow blue spike stands at the center, at 486.1 nanometers, much narrower than the hump."
#| fig-height: 3.8

rng = np.random.default_rng(206)
lam0 = 486.1
n_clouds = 4000
# Clouds on circular orbits at a range of radii, speed falling as r^(-1/2),
# with every orientation equally likely, so each one's line-of-sight speed is
# its orbital speed times the cosine of a random angle.
v_orb = 4500 * KMS * rng.uniform(0.6, 1.6, n_clouds) ** -0.5
v_los = v_orb * rng.uniform(-1, 1, n_clouds)
lam = np.linspace(478, 494, 1200)
dv = (lam / lam0 - 1) * C                 # velocity of each wavelength
width_cloud = 40 * KMS                    # each cloud's own small line width
profile = np.zeros_like(lam)
for v in v_los:
    profile += np.exp(-0.5 * ((dv - v) / width_cloud) ** 2)
profile /= profile.max()
narrow = np.exp(-0.5 * (dv / (250 * KMS)) ** 2)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 3.8))
for v in v_los[:14]:
    ax.plot(lam, 0.18 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((dv - v) / width_cloud) ** 2),
            color=ORANGE, lw=0.7, alpha=0.6)
ax.plot(lam, profile, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, zorder=3)
ax.plot(lam, 1.25 * narrow, color=BLUE, lw=2.0, zorder=4)
half = lam[profile >= 0.5]
ax.plot([half.min(), half.max()], [0.5, 0.5], color=INK2, lw=1.2)
ax.text(lam0, 0.54, "width", color=INK2, fontsize=9.5, ha="center")
ax.text(489.6, 0.9, "thousands of clouds\nin orbit: a broad line",
        color=ORANGE, fontsize=9.5, ha="left")
ax.text(484.9, 1.1, "a narrow line,\nfor comparison", color=BLUE,
        fontsize=9.5, ha="right")
ax.set_xlim(478, 494)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.4)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel(r"wavelength (nm), near H$\beta$")
ax.set_ylabel("brightness")
axv = ax.secondary_xaxis("top", functions=(lambda l: (l / lam0 - 1) * C / KMS,
                                           lambda v: lam0 * (1 + v * KMS / C)))
axv.set_xlabel(r"velocity along the line of sight (km s$^{-1}$)")
plt.show()
```

**How far out is the gas?** Nobody can see it; even in 3C 273, the
line-emitting gas is a few thousandths of a second of arc from the center, a
thousand times too small to resolve with an ordinary telescope. The trick is
the one we just used: light-travel time. The gas glows because the quasar's
light shines on it, so when the quasar brightens, the lines brighten too, but
only after the light has had time to reach the gas. Watch a quasar's continuum
and its lines for long enough, and the lines lag by a time $\tau$, which is the
distance of the gas divided by the speed of light. This is **reverberation
mapping** [@blandford1982], and after years of patient monitoring it has given
the sizes of the line-emitting regions of dozens of quasars and active galaxies
[@kaspi2000; @peterson2004]. The lags are weeks to a year: the gas is light-weeks
to a light-year out, a thousand or so Schwarzschild radii, far outside the disk
but far inside the galaxy. With $r = c\,\tau$ and $v$ from the width of the
line,

$$
M = f\, \frac{c\, \tau\, v^2}{G} ,
$$ {#eq-blr-mass}

where $f$ is a number near one that accounts for the clouds not all being on
circular orbits in one plane, and for the line's width being a particular
measure of the spread of speeds. Weighed this way, the black hole of 3C 273 is
about $9 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$ [@peterson2004], thirty times the minimum we
found from its light, and the quasar shines at a few percent of its Eddington
limit. In 2018 the gas was finally *seen* to orbit: combining the light of the
four 8-meter telescopes of the Very Large Telescope in Chile, the GRAVITY
instrument resolved the line-emitting region of 3C 273, about 150 light-days
in radius and rotating, with one side coming toward us and the other going
away, around a black hole of about $3 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$ [@gravity2018].
Lecture 19 does the same thing for the black hole at the center of the Milky
Way, where single stars can be followed around it.

Closer in still, the innermost part of the disk emits the iron line of lecture
16, broadened and skewed by orbital speeds near a third of the speed of light
and by the gravitational redshift. The broad hydrogen lines of this lecture and
the iron line of that one are the same effect at two distances: the Doppler
effect, reading out the orbits of gas around a black hole.

::: {.content-visible when-format="html"}

### Exercises {#sec-exercises-lines-mass}

1. In a quasar the H$\beta$ line is observed to lag the continuum by 100 days,
   and its width corresponds to a spread of speeds of
   $3000\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. Taking $f = 1$, what is the mass of the black
   hole in solar masses?

   ::: {.callout-tip .help-hint collapse="true" title="Hint, and the answer"}
   The radius is $r = c\,\tau$; convert the 100 days to seconds first, and
   the speed to centimeters per second. Then @eq-blr-mass is lecture 17's
   $rv^2/G$.

   The gas is $2.6 \times 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm}$ out, about $0.08\
   \mathrm{pc}$, and the mass is $3.5 \times 10^{41}\ \mathrm{g} =
   1.8 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$.
   :::

2. The line-emitting gas of 3C 273 is about $150$ light-days from a black
   hole of about $3 \times 10^{8}\,M_\odot$ (the GRAVITY result above). How
   fast does gas in a circular orbit move there, in kilometers per second? By
   how many nanometers would that speed shift the H$\beta$ line of a cloud
   coming straight toward us? How many Schwarzschild radii out is the gas?

   ::: {.callout-note .help-answer collapse="true" title="Answer"}
   The orbital speed is about $3200\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, which shifts
   H$\beta$ by about $5\ \mathrm{nm}$; the gas is about $4000$ Schwarzschild
   radii from the black hole.
   :::

3. The lines of a quiet galaxy's gas are a few hundred kilometers per second
   wide, and a quasar's broad lines are ten times wider. By what factor is the
   mass inside the orbit of the gas larger, if the gas is at the same radius?
   Which galaxy does lecture 17 let you weigh this way, at what radius?

4. Why does reverberation mapping take years of observing a single quasar?
   Think about what has to happen, and be seen to happen, before a lag can be
   measured, and about how long a lag of a hundred days is compared with how
   quickly quasars change.

:::

## Quasars then and now

The universe had far more quasars when it was young than it has today. The
number of luminous quasars per volume of space rose steeply through the first
few billion years after the Big Bang, peaked when the universe was about a
quarter of its present age, and has fallen by a large factor since
[@shen2020]. The brightest quasars we see are therefore mostly far away, and
seen as they were long ago: 3C 273, at $677\ \mathrm{Mpc}$, is one of the
closest there is.

Where did they all go? Lynden-Bell's answer in 1969 was that a quasar is a
phase, not a kind of object. A black hole shines as a quasar while gas is
falling into it, and when the supply runs out, after perhaps a hundred million
years, the light goes out, but the black hole stays, heavier than before. The
galaxies around us today should therefore be full of **dead quasars**: black
holes of millions to billions of solar masses, sitting quietly in the centers
of galaxies [@lyndenbell1969]. That prediction is what the rest of the course
tests. Lecture 19 finds the one at the center of our own Galaxy, from the
orbits of stars around it. Lecture 20 looks at the galaxies whose black holes
are still being fed, the active galactic nuclei, and at why they look so
different from one another. Lecture 21 asks how the masses of these black
holes are tied to the galaxies they live in, and lecture 22 returns to the jet
of 3C 273.

## If you want to go further

None of this section is needed for what comes before or after.

**Kutner, §19.4 to §19.6.** The chapter PDF in Canvas Files tells the
discovery story of §*The discovery of quasars* at more length, including the
decades-long argument over whether quasars were really as far away as their
redshifts say (§19.4.3), the quasars that gravitational lensing splits into
several images (§19.5), and the "unified picture" of active galaxies
(§19.6), which lecture 20 takes up. Its end-of-chapter problems 19.4, 19.7,
19.8, 19.9, 19.13 and 19.16 are on this lecture's material, and use
$H_0 = 70\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ as we do.

::: {.callout-warning .textbook-watch title="Textbook watch: when black holes were proposed for quasars"}
Kutner's §19.4.3 says that *"when it was suggested in the 1980s that quasars
might involve some form of black hole, the idea was not taken seriously by
most."* The dates are off by two decades. Salpeter and Zel'dovich proposed
accretion onto massive black holes as the power source in 1964, within a year
of Schmidt's paper [@salpeter1964], and Lynden-Bell's 1969 paper
[@lyndenbell1969] made the case in detail, including the prediction of dead
quasars in the nuclei of ordinary galaxies. The idea took time to win over
everyone, but it was on the table from the start.
:::

**Seeing the gas orbit.** The GRAVITY Collaboration's paper [-@gravity2018]
is short, and its one figure, the shift of the line-emitting region's
position from the red side of the line to the blue side, is the first direct
picture of gas orbiting a quasar's black hole.

**The first quasar papers.** The four papers in the 16 March 1963 issue of
*Nature* that announced 3C 273 and 3C 48 [@hazard1963; @schmidt1963; @oke1963;
@greenstein1963] are each a page or two long, and still readable.

## Summary

| idea | result | why it matters |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Spectral lines | emission lines from thin hot gas, at wavelengths set by the atom | the pattern of lines identifies the gas and gives its redshift |
| The discovery | 3C 273's lines are hydrogen's, all shifted by $1 + z$ with $z = 0.158$ | a star-like object far beyond the galaxies |
| Hubble's law | $v = H_0 D$, so $D = cz/H_0$ with $H_0 = 70\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ | a redshift is a distance (for $z \lesssim 0.2$) |
| Luminosity | $L = 4\pi D^2 F$; 3C 273 gives off $10^{12}\,L_\odot$ in visible light | brighter than whole galaxies |
| Size | $R \lesssim c\,\Delta t$; days of variability mean light-days of size | the light comes from a region the size of the Solar System |
| Mass | $M > L\sigma_T/4\pi c G m_p$, the Eddington minimum | tens of millions of solar masses at least |
| Why a black hole | that much mass in that little space, shining at up to tens of percent of $mc^2$ | nothing else can do it; Salpeter and Zel'dovich 1964, Lynden-Bell 1969 |
| Broad lines | $M = f\,c\tau v^2/G$ from the line width and the reverberation lag | weighs the black hole: $\sim 10^{9}\,M_\odot$ for 3C 273 |
| Then and now | quasars peaked when the universe was a quarter of its age | today's galaxies hold dead quasars |

A quasar is a supermassive black hole caught eating. The black hole is the
same one lecture 9 grew and lecture 17 weighed at the center of the Milky Way,
and next time we go there: the stars that orbit Sagittarius A\* so closely
that we can watch them go around, and what they tell us about the four million
solar masses at the center of our own Galaxy.
